concerns.text: The plan defers power analysis to the implementation phase ('[deferred]') and assumes a sample size > 1,000 is sufficient. For a multi-class classification task with potentially hundreds of space group classes (high cardinality) and a scaffold-based split (which reduces effective sample size per class), 1,000 samples may be statistically underpowered to detect meaningful signal above the majority-class baseline. The methodology risks producing a false negative (concluding no signal exists) due to insufficient sample size rather than a true lack of predictive capability.

The plan treats (SMILES, Space Group) pairs as distinct samples to handle polymorphism. However, if the dataset contains many molecules with identical SMILES but different space groups, the model is forced to predict a distribution of outcomes from a single input feature vector. Standard classification metrics (Accuracy/F1) will inherently penalize the model for this ambiguity, potentially masking any true topological signal. The methodology needs to explicitly define how to handle this 'one-to-many' mapping in the loss function or evaluation metric (e.g., treating it as a multi-label task or using a specific uncertainty metric) to validly assess the 2D->3D signal.

The plan relies on direct download of the COD organic subset. The methodology does not specify a filtering strategy for 'inorganic' entries beyond checking for non-C/H/N/O/S/P atoms. Many organic crystals in COD contain metal catalysts or counter-ions (e.g., Na+, Cl-) which are essential for the crystal structure but would be filtered out by a strict 'organic-only' heuristic, potentially biasing the dataset or losing valid samples. The construct validity of the 'organic subset' is at risk if the filtering logic is too aggressive or too loose.
